newsitem.title: CANADA: De Gaulle's Quebec visit honored 30 years later.
newsitem.headline: De Gaulle's Quebec visit honored 30 years later.

text.p: Thirty years after Charles de Gaulle's controversial speech galvanised a generation of Quebec separatists, his words on Thursday echoed once again from the city hall balcony where he first pronounced them.

Several hundred supporters of Quebec independence gathered in front of the stone building as the general's declaration -- "Vive le Quebec libre" (Long live a free Quebec) -- was played over loudspeakers.
The carefully staged moment was the culmination of two days during which Quebec separatists celebrated de Gaulle's visit to Quebec in 1967 when he was France's president.
The general's balcony speech spurred separatist sentiments in Quebec just as Canada was celebrating its centennial and sparked a diplomatic storm between Ottawa and Paris.
Thursday's event was organised by Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste, a Quebec nationalist organisation, but it included Quebec government officials.

Messages from French political leaders were also read to the throng, including one from Philippe Seguin, president of the Rassemblement pour la Republique (RPR) and personal envoy of French President Jacques Chirac.
And Pierre Messmer, who was defence minister under de Gaulle, recalled the general's famous words.
"This message was quite simple. It consisted of affirming that .. the right of the Quebec people to decide its own future is an inalienable right," Messmer said.

Bernard Landry, deputy Prime Minister in the French-speaking province's separatist Parti Quebecois government, said de Gaulle's speech inspired him when he was among the tens of thousands of people who first cheered it from the streets below City Hall.
"Hope has been replaced by the certainty that our people will be independent," Landry said.
In October 1995 separatists narrowly lost a second referendum on Quebec sovereignty. The Quebec government has said it will hold another referendum if it wins the next provincial election.

Thursday's ceremony was more calm than one on Wednesday in the provincial capital Quebec City, during which Canadian war veterans tried to drown out speeches made at the unveiling of a bronze statue of de Gaulle.
